seo.title: Karmic tail 15 5 17 compatibility: The Devil, The Hierophant, The Star
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 5 17 compatibility: a secret bond at the entry, life by others' rules in the middle and The Star as the main task. What it asks of a couple.

title: Karmic tail 15-5-17 in compatibility: a scarlet letter for two
short: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, the word for which Hester Prynne wears a scarlet "A" on her breast is never written once. Instead, the letter itself manages to be three cards over the course of the novel: the Black Man's mark, the community's sentence and a sign in the night sky. The couple's karmic tail 15-5-17 is the same three cards, The Devil, The Hierophant and The Star: the union begins as a bond only the two of them know about, lives inside rules and roles, and learns to be true in daylight.

sections.h2: A letter without a word: the story and why it fits this tail
paragraphs: Boston in the 1640s. A young woman is led out of prison onto the scaffold of the pillory. In her arms is a three-month-old daughter; on her breast is a scarlet "A" she embroidered herself in gold thread, so lavishly that the mark of shame looks like an ornament. Hester Prynne will not name the child's father. The father is standing right there, on the balcony above the scaffold: the young minister Arthur Dimmesdale, the pride of the town, and it is he whom the elders ask to persuade her to name the man. Her husband, long thought lost, is standing in the crowd. He will call himself Roger Chillingworth, become the minister's "leech", as the novel calls him, and spend seven years slowly drawing the secret out of him. Then come a meeting in the forest, a plan to escape by ship, a holiday sermon and a confession on the same scaffold.

Hawthorne never writes the word the letter stands for. Its root appears in the book exactly once, and not where one would expect it: in the very first scaffold scene, old Reverend Wilson blinks "in the unadulterated sunshine". Adulterate and the word for Hester's offence come from the same Latin verb, "to corrupt, to falsify". Hawthorne had named the word outright earlier, in the story "Endicott and the Red Cross": there a woman wears the same "A", embroidered so skilfully that it "might have been thought to mean 'Admirable,' or anything rather than 'Adulteress.'" In the novel Hawthorne removes the word and keeps the letter. And a letter without a word is read by everyone in their own way.

There are three readings in the novel, and they come in the order of the tail. In the forest Hester tells her daughter: "Once in my life I met the Black Man! This scarlet letter is his mark!" — the Black Man being the Puritans' name for the devil. The town that passed the sentence decides, seven years later, that the "A" means "Able". And on the night the governor dies, a meteor flares across the sky, and the next morning the sexton tells the minister about "a great red letter in the sky,—the letter A, which we interpret to stand for Angel." The mark, the community's sentence, the sign in the sky: The Devil, The Hierophant, The Star.

There is also a sentence in which Hawthorne himself puts all three cards in their places. When Hester throws off the letter in the forest, sunlight floods the woods, and he writes: "Such was the sympathy of Nature—that wild, heathen Nature of the forest, never subjugated by human law, nor illumined by higher truth—with the bliss of these two spirits!" The forest, with neither law nor higher truth, is The Devil. Human law is The Hierophant. Higher truth is The Star. The whole novel moves between three places: the forest, the town with its church and scaffold, and the sky above.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: "We said so to each other"
paragraphs: M, "Entry to the task", is what the couple wants together: its wishes, its agreements, its common language. On the site this point carries two captions: in the sphere "Relationship and common language" the same card appears as "Common language". For a 15-5-17 couple, the common language is The Devil.

In the novel this language can be heard in a single line. After seven years of silence, Hester and Arthur meet in the forest, and she whispers: "What we did had a consecration of its own. We felt it so! We said so to each other! Hast thou forgotten it?" — "No; I have not forgotten!" That is The Devil at the entry: the two have a consecration of their own that nobody else recognises, and a law of their own to live by. Such a bond has two witnesses, and it holds on secrecy.

Hawthorne finds a phrase for it that fits The Devil better than any interpretation: "Here was the iron link of mutual crime, which neither he nor she could break. Like all other ties, it brought along with it its obligations." The chain here runs not from people to a master but from one person to the other. Waite, surveying older decks, praises exactly this detail: in Papus the two human figures under The Devil are "yoked only to each other", and, Waite adds, "the author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." For a couple's tail this is more precise than a chain to an altar: there is no master, and yet there is no freedom.

The second chain in the novel is a pact of silence. In prison her husband makes Hester promise not to reveal who he is, and she asks: "Art thou like the Black Man that haunts the forest round about us? Hast thou enticed me into a bond that will prove the ruin of my soul?" — "Not thy soul," he answered, with another smile. "No, not thine!" Hester keeps his secret, the minister keeps his own, and the whole structure of the novel stands on two silences.

The couple's numbers say the same thing: The Devil appears between the two. Neither partner has 15 at the entry of their own tail — there it is 6 and 9, or 12 and 3. But in two thirds of these couples the outer cards of the tail already lie inside the partners: one has the personal tail 9-15-6, the other 6-17-11, The Devil in the middle of one and The Star in the middle of the other. These are not the roles of "the dark one" and "the bright one" — a personal tail is read by its own rules. But the union is literally stretched between two personal middles.

In life this entry shows in the first months. The two quickly become "us", and a little "us against everyone": nobody at work knows, the parents find out last, the couple has its own jokes and words that cannot be translated for outsiders. Sometimes the union really is born in spite of something — an age gap, a previous marriage, a different faith, a disapproving family. Sometimes there is no "in spite of" at all, only a pull after which it is hard to imagine oneself apart. At its best this entry gives something rare: the two accept each other's dark side, are not frightened by each other's desires, and know how to forgive. At its worst love speaks the language of ownership: the partner's phone must lie face up because "we have nothing to hide", and an evening with friends without the other is grounds for a week of hurt.

So the entry here is also resistance. A secret world for two is cosy, and every step into the light feels like betraying "us": telling a friend means giving it away, introducing the parents means handing it over for judgement. Hawthorne's minister chooses the secret for seven years for exactly this reason: as long as nobody knows about the bond, it belongs only to them.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Hierophant: the pastor and his parishioner
paragraphs: Chapter seventeen, the meeting in the forest, is called "The Pastor and His Parishioner". The two are alone together for the first time in seven years, and the chapter still calls them by their offices. This is how the middle of this tail is lived. N, "Middle of the task", shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task, and for 15-5-17 the road runs through The Hierophant: through form, rite, roles and someone else's "the proper way".

In town these two have no other language. When the governor and the ministers decide to take Hester's daughter away, she turns to Dimmesdale: "Speak thou for me! Thou wast my pastor, and hadst charge of my soul, and knowest me better than these men can." He can speak up for her only as a pastor — and he does: eloquently, theologically, and the girl is left with her mother. Everything that binds them in public passes through his office. Pearl, at seven, says it more plainly than any adult: "But here, in the sunny day, and among all the people, he knows us not; nor must we know him!"

Benebell Wen describes The Hierophant almost as a portrait of Dimmesdale: "a holy man, an important figure in his society, the interpreter of sacred mysteries. People rely on him to be a channel between heaven and earth." The minister knows this about himself and suffers for it. Again and again he climbs into the pulpit meaning to say: "I, your pastor, whom you so reverence and trust, am utterly a pollution and a lie!" — and every time he says only, vaguely, that he is the worst of sinners. His congregation listens and reveres him all the more.

Hester lives inside the same form, only from the other side. She earns her living with her needle, and her embroidery turns up at every rite of the colony: on the governor's ruff, on the ministers' bands, on babies' caps, in coffins. Hawthorne notes a single exception: she was never once called on to embroider "the white veil which was to cover the pure blushes of a bride." Every rite is open to her except the wedding. In Waite's list of meanings for The Hierophant, marriage is the first word.

Waite calls The Hierophant "the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature." The novel is built along the same border: the town with its institutions and the forest "never subjugated by human law". A couple with this tail lives on that border: in the forest it has truth without form, in town it has form without truth.

The arithmetic of the tail explains why the middle holds so hard. A couple's middle is not derived from the outer numbers; it is the sum of the two personal middles. But for 15-5-17 that sum is always the same: in all four combinations of personal tails the two middles add up to exactly 32 (15 + 17, 20 + 12, 19 + 13, 14 + 18), and 32 reduces to 5. The ends of the tail itself give the same: 15 + 17 = 32 → 5. This couple's Hierophant is literally made of The Devil and The Star, and in two thirds of couples also of two people — of one partner's middle (15) and the other's (17). **The form of the union is built from secrecy and truth**, and the question of the middle is which of the two it serves.

In life the middle shows at the family table. At home the two are one way; at the parents' they are a model couple: the right words, the right roles, "this is how we do things", a photo for the family chat. The real conversation starts in the car on the way home. The wedding is arranged the way the mothers want, the holidays are split according to someone else's timetable, one starts teaching the other how to live because "that's the right way". This is The Hierophant at its worst: someone else's rulebook in one's own home. At its best the five has another face. The couple gets its own holidays and rules that nobody imposed, and the partner also becomes a friend one can argue with about the things that matter.

Hawthorne shows this side too. Seven years on, the town no longer sees only shame in the letter. Hester goes into houses where there is trouble, sits with the sick, and many people begin to say the "A" means "Able". The form is the same; life has put the meaning into it. The Hierophant is not this couple's enemy: a rite, a rule, a shared order can become a vessel. Trouble begins when the vessel is empty and the outside looks lovely.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Tower: the card the tail jumps over
paragraphs: In the Major Arcana, cards 15, 16 and 17 stand side by side: The Devil, The Tower, The Star. The couple's tail goes from 15 straight to 17; the sixteenth is missing. It stands somewhere else: in 79.6% of couples with this tail, the centre is 16, The Tower. The couple's centre is "The atmosphere inside the couple" — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. **The skipped card is hidden inside the union.**

Both authors this reading relies on place The Tower between the chain and the star. Wen writes that The Star comes in the Major Arcana "after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower," and "after the downfall of The Tower, The Star is an indication of a turn upward." About The Tower itself she has a four-word sentence: "The aftermath is truth." Waite specifies what collapses: not just any house, but "the rending of a House of Doctrine" — more exactly, "a House of Falsehood". And he compares The Tower with The Devil: the one "is concerned with the fall into the material and animal state, while the other signifies destruction on the intellectual side." First the chain, then lightning on a false building, then the star.

In Hawthorne, The Tower is the night of chapter twelve. At midnight the minister climbs the scaffold of his own accord, and Hawthorne asks on his behalf: "Was it but the mockery of penitence?" Hester and Pearl climb up to him, all three join hands, and "the three formed an electric chain." Pearl asks: "Wilt thou stand here with mother and me, to-morrow noontide?" He refuses, and finally says: "But the daylight of this world shall not see our meeting!" — and at that moment the sky flares with a meteor. The street is lit "with the distinctness of mid-day", and the three stand on the scaffold "as if it were the light that is to reveal all secrets, and the daybreak that shall unite all who belong to one another." Next morning the town talks about the letter in the sky, while the three on the scaffold, in the meteor's light, are seen by Chillingworth, standing "at no great distance": the light that should unite falls first to the keeper of the secret.

The atmosphere of such a couple often resembles that night: inside, they know where the crack is, and they live under a sky that may flare up. At its worst, a quarrel brings "then I'll leave" — not as a decision but as a lever, and both remember every word for years. At its best, The Tower at the centre is one of the strongest supports: when a real upheaval comes, a lost job or a move, such a couple does not panic but stands shoulder to shoulder, and the shock binds them. Among The Tower's tasks Lisovskaya names one this tail needs directly: to survive the collapse of an invented image of the partner. What falls is the picture, not the people.

In the remaining 20.4% of couples the centre is The Chariot. Hawthorne has it too — the ship that sails for Bristol "within three days' time", on which Hester has already arranged "the passage of two individuals and a child". An atmosphere of movement: leave, start over, decide fast. The Chariot can carry a couple away, but it does not solve the tail's task for them: these two never sail for Bristol.

sections.h2: Main task — The Star: three scaffolds
paragraphs: D, "Main task", is read mostly through what the couple does not manage. For 15-5-17 it is The Star, and its task can be put simply: **to be the same in private and in public**. The Star is open light. Its trouble is light for show.

The scaffold appears three times in the novel, and it shows how the task gets solved. The first time, at noon, the magistrates put Hester on it: that is form and sentence. The second time, at midnight, the minister climbs it himself, but where nobody sees: a secret playing at penance. The third time, at noon again, after the holiday sermon, he calls Hester and Pearl himself, climbs up with them before the whole town and tears the ministerial band from his breast. "It was revealed!"

Just before that, Hawthorne shows The Star at its worst in full glitter. The Election Day sermon is the height of Dimmesdale's fame: "never had man spoken in so wise, so high, and so holy a spirit." Here The Star does not shine, it sparkles: adoration instead of closeness, an audience instead of someone to talk to. In a couple this Star shows in small things. There are holiday photos, but no conversation about what happened on holiday. The partner is praised in front of guests and quietly corrected at home to fit one's own image. They are loved as an admirer, while their own dream — a move, a course, a business — is somehow always badly timed. They are compared with other couples in the feed.

There is a subtler clue. In the forest the minister kisses Pearl on the brow, and the girl runs to the brook and washes the kiss away. On the scaffold, in front of everyone, he asks: "Dear little Pearl, wilt thou kiss me now? Thou wouldst not, yonder, in the forest! But now thou wilt?" — "Pearl kissed his lips. A spell was broken." Hawthorne calls the girl "the connecting link between those two". What a couple has created together will not accept a love that is ashamed of daylight — and lives by The Star's law before the couple does.

Hawthorne puts the moral into a single sentence: "Be true! Be true! Be true! Show freely to the world, if not your worst, yet some trait whereby the worst may be inferred!" He does not demand that everything be put on display. He demands that nothing be faked. The word freely also stands in the motto Waite gives The Star: "Waters of Life freely".

The most exact clue is a single phrase. The words "her own free will" occur in the novel twice — in the first scene and in the last. On the prison threshold Hester pushes the beadle away and steps into the open air "as if by her own free will." In the last chapter, many years later, she comes back to Boston herself and, "of her own free will, for not the sternest magistrate of that iron period would have imposed it," puts the letter on again. **Between "as if by her own free will" and "of her own free will" lies this whole tail.**

And the letter changes its meaning one last time: it "ceased to be a stigma" and was "looked upon with awe, yet with reverence too." Women come to Hester with their troubles in love, and she tells them a time will come when "a new truth would be revealed, in order to establish the whole relation between man and woman on a surer ground of mutual happiness." Wen writes that The Star can represent "someone who is a spiritual counselor, who shares his or her spirituality with others to restore hope and inspire others." That is Hester after everything: not a star of the stage, but a light people come to.

For a couple, The Star at its best looks ordinary. The two say plainly to each other what they like and what they do not. They are not shy of their feelings in public and do not perform them. They help each other work out who each wants to be, and do not stand in the way, even when the partner's dream is inconvenient. Their pretty picture is the truth: at home and at the parents' they are the same people.

sections.h2: The forest is not a way out: why throwing off the letter is not enough
paragraphs: The most treacherous scene in the novel is the brightest one. In the forest Hester says: "See! With this symbol, I undo it all, and make it as it had never been!" — unfastens the clasp and throws the letter among the withered leaves. "She had not known the weight, until she felt the freedom!" She takes off her cap, her hair falls to her shoulders, and sunlight floods the woods; the chapter is called "A Flood of Sunshine". The two agree to flee. It seems that here at last is The Star: freedom, light, the truth of feeling.

But this is still the forest, the one "never subjugated by human law, nor illumined by higher truth." Freedom here is The Devil again: the secret of two is not to be opened but carried away. And Pearl will not cross the brook to her mother. Hester says: "Bring it hither!" — "Come thou and take it up!" answers the girl, and her mother fastens the letter back on her breast. Hawthorne does not give the couple a Star won by running: the light comes only on the scaffold at noon.

For a 15-5-17 couple this is the tail's main warning. When the middle presses — family, rules, roles — it is easy to resolve it by going backwards, to the entry: fall out with the family for good, move away, "drop everything", shut themselves in as two again. That is relief, not a solution. The Star asks not to throw off the form but to make it true — to bring into town what was true in the forest.
What changes the script:

ul: **Tell private from secret.** The Star does not ask a couple to put its life on display: for Lisovskaya too much openness is also one of The Star's weaknesses. It asks that there be no two versions — one for home, another for other people.
**Say at the table what is usually said in the car.** One thing, calmly and without a challenge. The test of this tail is simple: is the couple at the table the same as the couple on the drive home?

**Ask each other what form of union each partner wants** — wedding, holidays, faith, children, money — separately from what the parents want. The Hierophant at its best is rules the two have made up themselves.
**Keep no pacts of silence against each other.** When one knows and the other is bound to keep it, that is Chillingworth's chain, not closeness.
**Do not stand in the way of the other's light.** Support the partner's work, dream and growth; do not make them dependent or turn them into an admirer.

paragraphs: If the bond rests on fear, threats, surveillance or violence, it is no longer a question of cards. In danger, call the local emergency number; a psychologist or a crisis line can help sort it out.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the world, a turned-around view, a garden
paragraphs: The sphere "The couple's values" is the couple's spiritual purpose, the road the two are to walk together. Couples with the 15-5-17 tail most often have one of three cards there:

ul: **21, The World — 50.4% of couples.** In the forest Hester asks: "Is the world, then, so narrow? Doth the universe lie within the compass of yonder town...?" The World among the values answers her in its own way: the world is wide, but its hardships are crossed together, not run away into. A broad view, a shared outlook, no pressure on each other.

**12, The Hanged Man — 24.8%.** The ability to look at the same sign from the other side, like the town that read the "A" as "Able". Tact, patience, care — and a danger this tail knows well: a flawless picture outside and heaviness inside.

**3, The Empress — 24.7%.** What grows: a home, children, a shared business, a craft. In Hawthorne it is Hester's needle, the rose-bush by the prison door, and Pearl in her scarlet dress — "the scarlet letter endowed with life!"

sections.h2: How 15-5-17 comes about: a worked example
paragraphs: The example is the couple 14.05.1976 and 05.11.1975. The partners' personal tails are 9-15-6 and 6-17-11, the most common combination for this tail. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, reduced to 22:

The middle here is the sum of the two personal middles, 15 and 17, not a recalculation from the couple's outer numbers; that it equals the sum of the tail's ends is a feature of this particular tail. The couple's centre is 3 + 13 = 16, The Tower, as in four couples out of five. The couple's values are 3, The Empress. The Tower appears once more for this couple, at the point "What to create together" (5 + 11 = 16): what the two met for is also about the skill of building anew.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: one stone for two
paragraphs: Hawthorne ends the novel with a gravestone. The two are buried side by side, "yet with a space between, as if the dust of the two sleepers had no right to mingle. Yet one tombstone served for both." On it is a coat of arms and a device: "On a field, sable, the letter A, gules", a story "so sombre... and relieved only by one ever-glowing point of light gloomier than the shadow." Hawthorne honestly admits that this light is darker than shadow, but it is the only one and it never goes out. A scarlet point on a black field looks like a star at night.

The 15-5-17 tail promises the couple neither tragedy nor happiness. It shows where its light is: not in the secret and not in the rite, but in the two having nothing left to hide. **The strong version of this tail is a shared stone while still alive:** one truth for home and for other people, a space between two people who do not need to dissolve into each other, and one sign that is not shameful to show.

intro: The three points of a couple's tail are read in order, and the most important one is the last:

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** What the two want together: a bond just for themselves, a law of their own, a shared secret, attraction as their common language. The same wish later holds the couple in place.

**Middle of the task — 5, The Hierophant.** How the couple travels: through form — marriage, family, customs, roles, "the way things are done". The form can become a second chain, or it can become a vessel.
**Main task — 17, The Star.** What to learn: to be the same in private and in public, to give each other light without conditions, and not to swap the truth for a pretty picture.

intro: This is not a prediction and not a verdict. The numbers know nothing about affairs, secret romances or scandals. What is taken from the novel is not the characters' offence but the shape of their road: from a secret of two, through someone else's form, to a truth that no longer needs hiding.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-5-17 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix: The Devil at the entry to the task, The Hierophant in the middle, The Star as the main task. The union begins as a strong bond just for two, is lived through form — rules, roles, family — and learns to be the same in private and in public. The key point is The Star: truth without show. Lisovskaya also calls a couple's tail a karmic programme.

faq.q: Is it a sign of infidelity or a secret affair?
faq.a: No. Neither the cards nor the numbers say anything about affairs, secret marriages or scandals. The Scarlet Letter is a magnifying glass here: what is taken from the novel is the shape of the road, not the characters' offence. The secret at the entry can be entirely innocent — a common language others do not understand, or an attraction in which the two need nobody else.

faq.q: Do the couple's tails 17-5-15 or 5-15-17 exist?
faq.a: No. Of the numbers 15, 5 and 17, a couple's matrix produces only the order 15-5-17. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 5 and 17 cannot stand at the entry, and the permutation 15-17-5 does not occur for any couple.

faq.q: Why can't one person have the tail 15-5-17?
faq.a: In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre, and with a task of 17 the entry 15 cannot come out with any centre. If a couple were counted as one person, The Lovers would stand at its entry: 17 + 16 = 33 → 6, 17 + 7 = 24 → 6. A couple's entry is made of two personal entries (6 + 9 or 12 + 3), and in The Lovers' place stands The Devil — Wen calls the chained figures on that card "The Lovers from Key 6".

faq.q: What changes if the couple's centre is The Chariot rather than The Tower?
faq.a: The tail is the same; the atmosphere inside the couple changes. With The Tower at the centre (four couples in five), the two live under a sky that may flare up, and their strength is to survive the collapse of invented images together. With The Chariot (one couple in five), the atmosphere is movement, plans, moves and quick decisions, and the temptation to solve the tail's task by leaving is stronger.

About one couple in 223 (0.447%), 59th place out of 97 couple tails. In two thirds of cases it comes from the personal tails 6-17-11 and 9-15-6, less often from 6-20-14 and 9-12-3 (20%) or 12-19-7 and 3-13-10 (13%); the combination 6-14-8 and 9-18-9 produces it in less than one per cent of couples.

faq.q: Where is this tail in the compatibility reading?
faq.a: In the sphere "The couple's karmic tail": the three cards are captioned "Entry to the task", "Middle of the task" and "Main task". The Devil of the entry appears once more in the reading, as "Common language" in the sphere "Relationship and common language" — it is the same point of the couple.

The real conversation starts in the car on the way home. The wedding is arranged the way the mothers want, and one starts teaching the other how to live because "that's the right way". This couple's Hierophant is literally made of the two ends of the tail: 15 + 17 = 32, and 32 reduces to 5. **The form of the union is built from secrecy and truth**, and the whole question is which of the two it serves. Hawthorne shows this card's better side too: years later the town itself rereads the letter as "Able". The form is the same; life has put the meaning into it.

report.h3: The forest is not a way out

report: The most treacherous scene in the novel is the brightest one. Hester unfastens the clasp, throws the letter among the withered leaves, lets down her hair, and sunlight floods the woods. The two agree to flee by ship. Here, it seems, is The Star. But this is still the forest with neither law nor truth: the secret is not to be opened but carried away. The daughter will not cross the brook to her mother until the letter is back in its place: "Come thou and take it up!"

For a couple with this tail, this is the main warning. When the middle presses, it is easy to resolve it by going backwards, to the entry: fall out with the family for good, move away, shut themselves in as two again. That is relief, not a solution. The Star asks not to throw off the form but to make it true.

report.h3: Between "as if" and "of her own free will"

report: The scaffold stands in the novel three times. At noon the magistrates put Hester on it. At midnight the minister climbs it himself, where nobody sees, and tells the girl: "But the daylight of this world shall not see our meeting!" The last time, at noon again, at the height of his fame, he calls Hester and the girl up onto the scaffold himself, before the whole town. In the forest the daughter washed his kiss away in the brook; on the scaffold "Pearl kissed his lips. A spell was broken." What two people have created together will not accept a love that is ashamed of daylight.

Hawthorne fits the moral into a single line: "Be true! Be true! Be true!" Then comes: "Show freely to the world." He does not demand that everything be put on display; he demands that nothing be faked. And the words "her own free will" stand in the novel twice. In the first scene Hester leaves the prison "as if by her own free will." In the last, many years later, she comes back and, "of her own free will", puts the letter on again. **Between "as if by her own free will" and "of her own free will" lies this whole tail.**

The main task, The Star, sounds simple: **to be the same in private and in public**. Tell private from secret: do not put the couple's life on display, but do not keep two versions either, one for home and one for guests. Say at the table what is usually said in the car. Make up rules of one's own instead of someone else's rulebook. Keep no pacts of silence against each other, and do not stand in the way of the other's light — the partner's dream, work and growth. If the bond rests on fear, threats or violence, it is no longer a question of cards: in danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line, and a psychologist can help sort it out.
